nameStory: Leafy spurge gets its name from its abundance of narrow leaves that crowd along the stem, giving it a particularly leafy appearance compared to other spurges. The word 'spurge' comes from the old French 'espurgier,' meaning 'to purge,' referring to the plant's historical use as a harsh medicinal purgative.
description: Leafy spurge is a tall, upright perennial herb that can grow 1-4 feet high, forming dense patches through underground roots. It has narrow, blue-green leaves that spiral up sturdy stems, topped with clusters of small yellowish-green flowers surrounded by bright yellow bracts that look like petals. This European native has become an aggressive invader in parts of North America, though it's still relatively uncommon in New England with only 8 recorded observations.

idTips.label: Milky Sap
idTips.description: Break any part of the stem or leaf and a thick, white, latex-like sap immediately oozes out - this milky juice is caustic and can cause skin irritation, so avoid touching it

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellowish-green flowers lack petals but are surrounded by bright yellow, heart-shaped bracts that create showy clusters at the stem tips from late spring through summer

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves about 1-3 inches long with smooth edges, arranged alternately up the stem in a dense, spiraling pattern that gives the plant its leafy appearance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms upright colonies of multiple stems growing from creeping underground roots, often creating dense patches that crowd out other plants

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Three-chambered capsules that explosively pop open when ripe, shooting small gray seeds several feet away with an audible snapping sound

habitat: Look for leafy spurge in disturbed soils along roadsides, abandoned fields, and waste areas where it can establish without competition. It prefers well-drained, sandy or gravelly soils and full sun, often appearing near agricultural areas or along transportation corridors where seeds may have been accidentally introduced.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge early, showing the characteristic narrow leaves spiraling up reddish stems. The distinctive milky sap is present as soon as growth begins.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow flower clusters are most prominent from June through August, making this the easiest season for identification. Seeds begin forming in three-chambered capsules.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn reddish or orange before dying back, and mature seed capsules explosively release seeds. Above-ground parts begin to wither.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground roots, leaving only dried stem remnants. Look for old seed capsules and dried flower clusters as evidence of last year's growth.

funFact: When leafy spurge seed pods ripen, they explode with enough force to launch seeds up to 15 feet away, and the popping sound is actually audible if you're standing nearby - it's like nature's own tiny fireworks show!
confusionNotes: Leafy spurge is most easily confused with cypress spurge, but leafy spurge has broader, more lance-shaped leaves while cypress spurge has extremely narrow, almost needle-like leaves. Remember: leafy spurge is truly 'leafy' with wider leaves, while cypress spurge looks more like a tiny evergreen.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the same family as the popular holiday poinsettia, leafy spurge is considered a noxious weed in many western states where it's more common. The milky sap that's diagnostic for identification is also quite toxic and was historically used to burn off warts, earning spurges the nickname 'wart weed.'
compareHints: Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants. Unlike the tiny leaves of cypress spurge or the broad leaves of flowering spurge, leafy spurge has medium-width, lance-shaped leaves that crowd thickly along the stem.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves.
Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat.
Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters.
Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage.
Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form.
Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.
Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat.
Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves.
Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves.
Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves.
Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region.
Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright.
Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves.
Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name.
